South Korea’s Defense Space Strategy & Military Space Architecture

  • Defense
  • Government
  • LEO Satellite
  • Strategy

An analysis of South Korea’s Ministry of National Defense space strategy and military space architecture as of early November 2026. It covers Project 425’s completed 1 EO/IR + 4 SAR constellation, the KRW 1.4223 trillion microsatellite system (2022–2030), the satcom gap around ANASIS-II and its 2031–32 replacement, a March 2026 LEO satcom task force studying 128–512 satellites by about 2035, plus PNT, missile warning, SDA, launch and industrial-base roles. A 14-row program table ties each effort to contractors and sourced timelines.

South Korea’s Defense Space Strategy & Military Space Architecture

Analysis report — Ministry of National Defense (MND), JCS, ROK Air Force, DAPA, ADD and KASA programs | Status as of November 2, 2026

Prepared for Paul. Citations in square brackets are clickable and map to the numbered References. Items marked [UNVERIFIED] rest on a single non-official source or on conflicting reports.

1. Executive summary

  • Sovereign ISR is done; persistence comes next. The fifth and final Project 425 satellite (SAR) launched Nov 2, 2025, completing a 1 EO/IR + 4 SAR constellation worth about KRW 1.3 trillion [1,3]. The fifth satellite was reported to enter service by end-April 2026, about two months early, which gives roughly 2-hour revisit over North Korea [5,4].
  • The next phase is mass, from SAR microsatellite constellations. The multi-agency Microsatellite System (KRW 1.4223 trillion, 2022–2030, ADD-led) has a SAR verification satellite planned for 2H 2026 [13,14]. Hanwha Systems won the SAR satellite development contract on Oct 30, 2026 [15]. Military plans call for about 60 small and micro reconnaissance satellites by 2030, aiming at revisit of 30 minutes or less [11,5].
  • Responsive launch is about to be tested. ADD’s solid-fuel space launch vehicle (provisional name “Mir”) was scrubbed on June 30, 2026, and MND is targeting a launch by year-end [20]. Public launch trackers list it NET Nov 4, 2026, 05:00 UTC (Nov 4, 12:00 AM EST) [21]. Nuri’s 5th flight (Oct 7, 2026) succeeded, and KASA plans to carry military EO microsatellites on Nuri in 2031 [18,17].
  • Satcom is the biggest gap, and the biggest opening for LEO players. Korea has one dedicated military GEO satellite (ANASIS-II, 2020) [22]. The GEO follow-on, Military Satcom System-III (about KRW 1.27 trillion through 2032), only started in 2026 [26]. Korea has no LEO communications satellites. A government LEO Satcom Task Force (MSIT/MND/DAPA/KASA) launched in March 2026 with a phased plan from commercial networks to an independent network [28]. Constellation scenarios of 128–512 satellites are being studied for about 2035 [31].
  • The organization is maturing. The Air Force Space Operations Squadron (Dec 2022) became a Group (Jun 2024) [40,41], and a space operations wing is planned by 2030 [45]. In an Oct 2026 parliamentary audit, the JCS said it is preparing a Space Command and a JCS-centered space C2 structure, with an electromagnetic warfare unit in 2027 [43].
  • Space domain awareness (SDA) and counterspace are long-dated. Only the electro-optical EOSS is operational (since 2022) [46]. A radar space surveillance system and a high-power laser satellite-tracking system have approved requirements but are slated for 2040 [45]. Missile-warning satellites appear only as a JCS ambition [54].

2. Strategy, policy and governance

2.1 Defense-level strategy

Defense Space Strategy. MND’s Defense Space Development Committee, chaired by the defense minister, reviewed the first draft “defense space strategy” on Dec 9, 2022. It is the overarching document for goals, principles and service operating concepts, and its details were not disclosed [35]. A DAPA forum summary says the strategy was finalized in February 2023 [36]. The full text is not public, so this report cannot assess its content beyond these descriptions.

Defense Space Development Basic Plan / force roadmap. We found no public copy or official summary of a stand-alone MND “Defense Space (Force) Development Basic Plan” [UNVERIFIED as a published document]. The most detailed public roadmap is the Air Force’s Oct 2025 audit briefing [45]:

  • By 2030: space weather forecasting/warning system and the microsatellite system; a space operations wing (우주작전단).
  • By 2040: high-power laser satellite tracking system, radar space surveillance system, KPS (laser and radar requirements already approved).
  • By 2050: space-based space surveillance and debris-removal spacecraft (requirements under review).

JCS. The JCS created a Military Space Division in its Strategic Planning Directorate in January 2022. At its first joint military space seminar (May 2023), it said it would build reconnaissance satellites, missile early-warning satellites, the microsatellite system, KPS and a LEO communications satellite system in phases [54]. In October 2026 the JCS chairman told the National Assembly that the military “recognizes the need for a Space Command and is preparing for it.” The JCS also briefed plans to strengthen its space organization and set up a JCS-centered space C2 structure, with an EW unit in 2027 [43,44].

2.2 National framework

4th Space Development Promotion Basic Plan (2023–2027). The National Space Committee confirmed the plan on Dec 21, 2022, under the Space Development Promotion Act. It doubles government space R&D spending from KRW 730 billion (2021) to KRW 1.5 trillion by 2027. Its goals include unmanned space transport in the 2030s, crewed transport by 2045, and a lunar landing in 2032. One of its five missions is “space security”, including expanded national security space assets. The same session approved the Microsatellite System development plan (KRW 1.4223 trillion through 2030) [13].

KASA. The Korea AeroSpace Administration was established under a Special Act [38] and launched on May 27, 2024, in Sacheon [37]. It now co-owns defense-relevant programs: microsatellites, Nuri, KPS and the LEO satcom TF [14,28]. CSIS notes that the new agency is meant to centralize space programs previously spread across ministries [39].

2.3 U.S.–ROK space cooperation

  • U.S. Space Forces Korea (SPACEFOR-KOR) was activated at Osan in December 2022 as the USSF component to USFK [47].
  • Working-level space cooperation talks (Nov 2024) agreed an annual tabletop exercise and ROK participation in the U.S.-led Joint Commercial Operations (JCO) cell. They also agreed to speed up a shared missile early-warning system [48]. The first exercise, Polaris Lynx, was held May 1, 2025, between the ROK JCS and SPACEFOR-KOR and simulated GPS jamming and attacks on ROK satellites [49].
  • In March 2026 the Air Force chief met the USSF director of science & technology at the Space Operations Group (Osan) [42]. On the civil side, the State Department published a joint statement from the U.S.–ROK Civil Space Dialogue (Apr 2025) [50].

2.4 Budget (sourced figures only)

The final 2026 defense budget is KRW 65.8642 trillion (+7.5%). Force improvement gets KRW 19.9653 trillion, and defense R&D gets KRW 5.8396 trillion. The National Assembly added new funding for a Defense Space Certification Center and increased funding for Project 425 and Military Satcom System-III [51,52]. MSC-III received only KRW 250 million for 2026, inserted by the Assembly [26]. No consolidated MND space budget figure is published, so program totals below are the best available proxies.

3. Architecture by mission layer

3.1 ISR — the core of the architecture

Project 425 (ADD development, with KAI, Hanwha Systems and Satrec Initiative participating) [1]:

  • #1 EO/IR, launched Dec 1, 2023 (U.S. time) from Vandenberg on Falcon 9 [7].
  • #2 SAR, launched Apr 8, 2024 (KST) from Kennedy Space Center [8].
  • #3 SAR, launched Dec 21, 2024 (KST) from Vandenberg [9].
  • #4 SAR, launched Apr 22, 2025 (KST) from Cape Canaveral [10].
  • #5 SAR, launched Nov 2, 2025 (KST) from Cape Canaveral on the Bandwagon-4 rideshare [2,6]. It passed operational test & evaluation and was expected in full service by end-April 2026 [5].
  • SAR payloads are by Hanwha Systems [6]. The SAR satellites can reportedly identify objects as small as 30 cm [4], and the program cost was about KRW 1.3 trillion [3].

Follow-on mass. Plans call for about 60 small (<500 kg) and micro (<100 kg) reconnaissance satellites by 2030 [11]. The Korea Herald (Apr 2026) describes this as about 20 small plus about 40 microsatellites [5]. The program lines are reported differently across sources and may overlap [PARTLY UNVERIFIED]:

  • Microsatellite System (초소형위성체계). Joint program of MND/DAPA, KASA and the Korea Coast Guard, with ADD as lead research institution (KARI, ETRI, NSRI and SaTReC participating). It costs KRW 1.4223 trillion over 2022–2030 [13,14]. The SAR verification satellite is planned for 2H 2026, followed by SAR constellation and EO satellites [14]. Hanwha Systems won the SAR satellite development contract on Oct 30, 2026 [15]. The defense minister told the Cabinet on Oct 20, 2026, that four microsatellite systems would launch in 2031 [31]. Nuri flight 11 (2031) is slated to carry four EO reconnaissance microsatellites [17].
  • 40-satellite SAR constellation (“develop-first, select-later”). SatNews reports a KRW 1.2 trillion competition between KAI (with LIG) and Hanwha Systems (with Satrec Initiative). It cites requirements of sub-150 kg and 50 cm resolution, a target revisit of 20–30 minutes, and five launches (three on SpaceX, then Nuri) [16]. [UNVERIFIED: trade-press detail; how it relates to the official Microsatellite System is unclear.]
  • Classified small and micro SAR program. Seoul Economic Daily reports 19 satellites on seven solid-fuel SLV launches in 2026–27, with the main ground station at the Defense Intelligence Command and ground stations by LIG [12]. [UNVERIFIED: single source, unnamed officials. The schedule depends on the solid SLV, which has not yet flown in full configuration.]
  • Civil/dual-use NEONSAT (KASA). Satellites 2–6 (<100 kg, EO, 1 m panchromatic resolution) launched on Nuri on Oct 7, 2026. Five more are due in 2H 2027 for a 10-satellite constellation [18,19].

3.2 Communications

  • ANASIS-II is the first military-only GEO satcom satellite. It was launched Jul 20, 2020, on Falcon 9 [22,23] and built by Airbus as an F-35 offset [26]. Ground terminals (eight types) were produced by LIG Nex1 and Hanwha Systems under a KRW 888.5 billion contract through 2025 [24].
  • Military Satcom System-III (ANASIS-III). The basic development plan was approved by DAPA’s 175th Defense Project Promotion Committee on May 22, 2026: about KRW 1.27 trillion through 2032, with ADD as system integrator [25,26]. The space segment will use foreign partners, while the control and terminal segments (eight terminal types, some EMP-hardened) will be domestic. Prototype contracts are expected by March 2027 and launch around 2031–32, likely on SpaceX or Ariane. A key driver is the ITU rule on keeping the ANASIS-II orbital slot, which would otherwise have to be returned at end-2032 [26].
  • Commercial LEO for the military. ADD’s rapid-acquisition institute signed a KRW 39.8 billion project with Hanwha Systems (Nov 2023). It covers military gateways, small ground stations and terminals for commercial LEO satellites, with two years of development and a six-month pilot [27]. Starlink (via Starlink Korea) and OneWeb (via Hanwha Systems and KT Sat) were cleared for Korean service in May 2025 [32]. Military use of Starlink has not been confirmed in official sources.
  • Sovereign LEO (“K-LEO”). The LEO Satellite Communications TF (launched Mar 26, 2026) will assess demand, costs and international cooperation. DAPA described a phased path “from the initial use of commercial networks to the ultimate establishment of an independent network” [28]. A 6G LEO verification system (two satellites) is planned for 2030, funded at KRW 320 billion through 2030 [32,31]. Constellation scenarios under study are 128 satellites at 1,280 km, 256 at 888 km, or 512 at 1,280 km by about 2035 [31]. Hanwha Systems signed an MOU with MDA Space (Jan 26, 2026) to evaluate AURORA software-defined satellites for K-LEO [29]. It is also working with Telesat on Lightspeed-compatible terminals, following a Canada–Korea letter of intent on LEO communications [30].

3.3 PNT

KPS is KASA-led: KRW 3.72 trillion over 14 years from 2022, with eight satellites targeted by 2035 [33]. The first satellite slipped 20 months, from Dec 2027 to Sep 2029, because of navigation-payload development [34]. Its critical design review was planned for late Sep 2026 [33]. The Air Force roadmap lists KPS deployment by 2040 [45]. North Korean GPS jamming is the main operational driver behind both Polaris Lynx and the planned EW unit [49,43].

3.4 Missile warning

Korea has no space-based missile-warning program in development. The JCS lists early-warning satellites as a phased ambition [54]. The allies agreed in 2024 to speed up a shared early-warning system with the U.S. [48]. A Seoul Economic Daily report says the small-satellite cluster would also support “early warning” missions [UNVERIFIED] [12]. Near-term dependence on U.S. missile-warning data remains.

3.5 Space domain awareness

The Air Force’s EOSS (electro-optical satellite surveillance system) entered operational service in January 2022. It tracks objects below 700 km altitude within a 2,000 km radius of Seoul, using observatories nationwide [46]. Its operations sit with the Space Operations Group at Osan. The Group joined, or planned to join, the U.S. JCO cell [41,48]. Planned additions are the radar space surveillance system and the high-power laser satellite tracking system, both by 2040 with requirements approved, and space-based SDA by 2050 [45].

3.6 Launch

  • ADD solid-fuel SLV (“Mir”, provisional). Under development since 2021 [20]. Earlier tests ran Mar 30 and Dec 30, 2022, and an orbital test without the 2nd stage on Dec 4, 2023 [21]. The first full four-stage launch was cancelled in final stages on Jun 30, 2026. MND targets a 2026 launch [20], and trackers list NET Nov 4, 2026, from an offshore platform south of Jeju [21]. The roughly 500 kg LEO capacity comes from the tracker only [UNVERIFIED]. It is intended to launch future micro reconnaissance satellites [20].
  • Nuri (KSLV-II). Its 5th flight on Oct 7, 2026, deployed five NEONSATs (4th consecutive success, 80% overall). Hanwha Aerospace built the rocket and took part in operations [18]. The plan calls for at least one Nuri launch a year through 2032, with military EO microsatellites in 2031 [17].
  • Foreign launch. All Project 425 satellites and ANASIS-II flew on SpaceX [7,2,22]. Ministers have acknowledged that domestic vehicles alone cannot deploy a 128+ satellite LEO constellation [31].

3.7 Counterspace and resilience

The only openly acknowledged counterspace-adjacent capability is the planned high-power laser tracking system (2040) [45]. Resilience work centers on proliferated microsatellites [11], a planned EW unit (2027) linking civil and military jamming detection [43], the EMP-hardened MSC-III terminals [26], and allied exercises [49]. There is no published policy on offensive counterspace.

5. Assessment

Strengths

  • Sovereign high-resolution SAR/EO ISR is fielded on schedule [5], and the two-hour revisit is a credible baseline for Kill Chain targeting.
  • Strong state funding momentum: the 2026 defense budget is up 7.5%, with Assembly add-backs for space [51]. Industry is vertically integrating, with Hanwha covering launch, SAR, satcom terminals and an EO bus via Satrec [16,18].
  • Domestic launch is maturing (Nuri reliability, solid SLV imminent) and civil-military programs are institutionalized through KASA [18,14].

Gaps and risks

  • Satcom: a single dedicated GEO satellite, a GEO replacement around 2031–32, and no sovereign LEO before the 2030 demo [26,31].
  • Missile warning and SDA depend on the U.S. Radar and laser SDA are 2040-class programs [45,48].
  • Schedule risk: the solid SLV slipped from June 2026 [20], and KPS-1 slipped 20 months [34]. Microsatellite program reporting is inconsistent across sources [16,12,14].
  • No unified space command yet. Space C2 is split across the Air Force, JCS and Defense Intelligence Command [43,12].

Opportunities for LEO satcom / sovereign constellation players

  • Interim commercial LEO service for the military. DAPA’s stated phase one is using commercial networks [28]. Hanwha’s military gateway and terminal work for commercial LEO [27] is the integration route, and OneWeb already has a Hanwha distribution path [32].
  • K-LEO constellation (128–512 satellites, about 2035). Officials say foreign launch and partners are needed [31]. Platform providers (MDA AURORA via Hanwha [29]), Telesat Lightspeed interoperability [30], and payload, ground and user-terminal suppliers are all positioned.
  • MSC-III GEO space segment. Its space segment will be sourced through foreign cooperation, and the offset level is a selection factor [26]. Also, the classified and multi-agency SAR constellations need downlink and ground networks.

What to watch, 2026–2028

  • Nov 2026 onward: the ADD solid SLV full-configuration flight (NET Nov 4) [21,20], and the SAR microsatellite verification satellite launch (2H 2026 target) [14].
  • 2026–27: LEO TF findings and a K-LEO acquisition decision; MSC-III prime/prototype contracts (by Mar 2027) [28,26].
  • 2027: the JCS EW unit and Space Command design; the Air Force’s path to a space operations wing by 2030 [43,45].
  • 2H 2027: Nuri flight 6 completing NEONSAT [18]. 2028: start of mass microsatellite deployment per plan [11].
  • Ongoing: allied tabletop exercises and a shared early-warning system [49,48].

Caveats

  • Defense Space Strategy (2022/23) and any MND space force basic plan are not public. Their content is described only from official summaries.
  • Microsatellite and SAR constellation reporting conflicts across sources on size, cost and contractor structure. Items are flagged where single-sourced.
  • The defense minister’s name differs across 2026 sources (KASA Mar 2026 vs MoneyToday Oct 2026 translation), so this report avoids naming the minister for late-2026 statements.
  • The solid SLV date comes from public launch trackers. MND had not announced an exact date as of Oct 19, 2026 [20].
